Genre Combinations and AI-Coded Review Dimensions: Random-Intercept Logistic Models

1. Load data and align reviewer_id / book_id

book_id_mapping.csv was produced by match_book_ids.py, which matched every one of the 50,000 annotated reviews to goodreads_reviews_dedup.json on user_id = Reviewer ID and identical (whitespace-normalised) review text.

setwd("C:/Users/gujia/Downloads/annotation_run")

library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

df  <- read.csv("annotated_50000sample.csv", check.names = FALSE,
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
map <- read.csv("book_id_mapping.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                colClasses = c(book_id = "character", review_id = "character"))

df$row         <- seq_len(nrow(df)) - 1      # 0-based row index used by the Python script
df             <- merge(df, map, by = "row", all.x = TRUE, sort = TRUE)
df$reviewer_id <- df[["Reviewer ID"]]

table(df$match_type, useNA = "ifany")

          ambiguous          exact_text   exact_text+rating     fuzzy_text>=0.9 
                154               45959                  20                 574 
genre_disambiguated           prefix200           unmatched 
                  1                3269                  23 
# keep reviews that were aligned to a book_id
df <- df[!is.na(df$book_id) & df$book_id != "", ]

c(reviews   = nrow(df),
  reviewers = length(unique(df$reviewer_id)),
  books     = length(unique(df$book_id)))
  reviews reviewers     books 
    49823     12278     16159 
# how clustered is the data?
summary(as.vector(table(df$reviewer_id)))   # reviews per reviewer
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  1.000   1.000   2.000   4.058   5.000  78.000 
summary(as.vector(table(df$book_id)))       # reviews per book
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  1.000   1.000   2.000   3.083   3.000  89.000

2. Split Genre into combinations

Each ;-separated piece of the Genre cell is one combination, e.g. "fantasy, paranormal; fiction" → "fantasy, paranormal" and "fiction".

genre_list <- lapply(strsplit(df$Genre, ";"), trimws)
genre_list <- lapply(genre_list, function(x) x[x != ""])
combos <- sort(unique(unlist(genre_list)))

# syntactic variable names: "fantasy, paranormal" -> "fantasy_paranormal"
clean_name <- function(x) gsub("_+", "_", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", x))
data.frame(combination = combos, variable = clean_name(combos))
                              combination                             variable
1                                children                             children
2                         comics, graphic                       comics_graphic
3                     fantasy, paranormal                   fantasy_paranormal
4                                 fiction                              fiction
5  history, historical fiction, biography history_historical_fiction_biography
6                mystery, thriller, crime               mystery_thriller_crime
7                             non-fiction                          non_fiction
8                                  poetry                               poetry
9                                 romance                              romance
10                            young-adult                          young_adult

3. One-hot encoding

1 = the book has this combination, 0 = it does not.

for (cmb in combos) {
  df[[clean_name(cmb)]] <- as.integer(vapply(genre_list, function(g) cmb %in% g, logical(1)))
}

# rename outcome columns: "Absence of Naive Realism_AI" -> "Absence_of_Naive_Realism_AI"
ai_cols <- grep("_AI$", names(df), value = TRUE)
names(df)[match(ai_cols, names(df))] <- clean_name(ai_cols)

df$reviewer_id <- factor(df$reviewer_id)
df$book_id     <- factor(df$book_id)

# number of reviews per combination
colSums(df[clean_name(combos)])
                            children                       comics_graphic 
                                3975                                 2564 
                  fantasy_paranormal                              fiction 
                               29647                                48613 
history_historical_fiction_biography               mystery_thriller_crime 
                               11484                                23629 
                         non_fiction                               poetry 
                                1741                                  515 
                             romance                          young_adult 
                               37705                                31303 
write.csv(df, "annotated_50000sample_onehot_ids.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")

4. Random-intercept logistic models

\[ \operatorname{logit} P(Y_{ijk}=1) = \beta_0 + \sum_{g}\beta_g\,\text{Genre}_{g,k} + u_{j} + v_{k}, \qquad u_j \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\text{reviewer}}),\; v_k \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\text{book}}) \]

for review i written by reviewer j about book k. The two random intercepts absorb the non-independence of reviews written by the same reviewer and reviews of the same book.

ctrl <- glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))

# nAGQ = 0: fast approximation used for the main results (nAGQ = 1 = Laplace, compared in Section 8)
NAGQ <- 0
dir.create("models", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Fit a model, or load it if it was already fitted (fit_glmm_parallel.R fits all 7 in parallel).
# For nAGQ = 1 the nAGQ = 0 estimates are used as starting values.
fit_glmm <- function(name, formula, nAGQ = NAGQ) {
  path <- if (nAGQ == 0) sprintf("models/%s_nagq0.rds", name) else
    sprintf("nAGQ1/models/%s_nagq%d.rds", name, nAGQ)
  if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  start <- NULL
  path0 <- sprintf("models/%s_nagq0.rds", name)
  if (nAGQ > 0 && file.exists(path0)) {
    m0 <- readRDS(path0)
    start <- list(theta = getME(m0, "theta"), fixef = fixef(m0))
  }
  m <- glmer(formula, data = df, family = binomial, control = ctrl, nAGQ = nAGQ, start = start)
  saveRDS(m, path)
  m
}

g1 <- fit_glmm("g1",
               Absence_of_Naive_Realism_AI ~ 1 + children + comics_graphic + fantasy_paranormal +

                 non_fiction + poetry + romance + young_adult +
                 (1 | reviewer_id) + (1 | book_id))

5. Tables

Fixed effects are reported on the log-odds scale and as odds ratios (OR) with Wald 95% CIs. OR > 1: reviews of books with this genre combination are more likely to be coded 1.

make_table <- function(model, outcome) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(model)))
  names(ct) <- c("log_odds", "std_error", "z_value", "p_value")
  ct$term     <- rownames(ct)
  ct$OR       <- exp(ct$log_odds)
  ct$OR_lower <- exp(ct$log_odds - 1.96 * ct$std_error)
  ct$OR_upper <- exp(ct$log_odds + 1.96 * ct$std_error)
  ct$sig <- as.character(cut(ct$p_value, breaks = c(-Inf, .001, .01, .05, Inf),
                             labels = c("***", "**", "*", "")))
  ct$outcome <- outcome
  ct$n <- nobs(model)
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
  ct[, c("outcome", "term", "log_odds", "std_error", "z_value", "p_value", "sig",
         "OR", "OR_lower", "OR_upper", "n")]
}

make_re_table <- function(model, outcome) {
  vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
  v_rev  <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "reviewer_id"]
  v_book <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "book_id"]
  total  <- v_rev + v_book + pi^2 / 3          # latent-scale residual variance of logit
  data.frame(outcome = outcome,
             var_reviewer = v_rev, var_book = v_book,
             ICC_reviewer = v_rev / total, ICC_book = v_book / total)
}

6. Graphs

genre_vars <- c("children", "comics_graphic", "fantasy_paranormal", "fiction",
                "history_historical_fiction_biography", "mystery_thriller_crime",
                "non_fiction", "poetry", "romance", "young_adult")

genre_labels <- c("Children", "Comics & Graphic", "Fantasy & Paranormal", "Fiction",
                  "History / Biography", "Mystery / Thriller / Crime", "Non-fiction",
                  "Poetry", "Romance", "Young Adult")

make_plot_data <- function(res) {
  res %>%
    filter(term %in% genre_vars) %>%
    mutate(significance = ifelse(sig == "", "ns", sig),
           term = factor(term, levels = genre_vars, labels = genre_labels))
}

plot_or <- function(res, title) {
  ggplot(make_plot_data(res), aes(x = OR, y = term)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = OR_lower, xmax = OR_upper), width = 0.2, orientation = "y") +
    geom_point(aes(color = significance), size = 3) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("***" = "#B2182B", "**" = "#EF8A62",
                                  "*" = "#67A9CF", "ns" = "gray65"),
                       drop = FALSE) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = paste0("Random intercepts for reviewer and book (nAGQ = ", NAGQ, ")"),
         x = "Odds Ratio (log scale, 95% CI)", y = "Genre Combination",
         color = "Significance") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
          legend.position = "bottom")
}

  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +

7. Summary

7.1 Data alignment

mt <- table(read.csv("book_id_mapping.csv")$match_type)
n_rev  <- length(unique(df$reviewer_id))
n_book <- length(unique(df$book_id))
  • Of the 50,000 annotated reviews, 49,823 were aligned to a Goodreads book_id via goodreads_reviews_dedup.json (99.6%). 45,979 matched on identical text, 3,269 on the first 200 characters, and 574 by fuzzy text similarity (≥ 0.90) within the same reviewer, rating and genre set. For every matched review the raw rating equals the star rating and the book’s genre set equals the Genre cell, which confirms the alignment.
  • 177 reviews could not be aligned uniquely (the same reviewer posted identical text for several books, or no match) and are excluded.
  • The analysed data contain 12,278 reviewers and 16,159 books.

7.2 Clustering: who writes the review vs. which book is reviewed

re_show <- re_all
re_show$ICC_total <- re_show$ICC_reviewer + re_show$ICC_book
knitr::kable(re_show[, c("outcome", "var_reviewer", "var_book", "ICC_reviewer", "ICC_book", "ICC_total")],
             digits = 3, col.names = c("Construct", "Var reviewer", "Var book",
                                       "ICC reviewer", "ICC book", "ICC total"))
Construct Var reviewer Var book ICC reviewer ICC book ICC total
Absence_of_Naive_Realism 0.616 0.192 0.150 0.047 0.197
Theme 0.808 0.218 0.187 0.051 0.238
Thought_Provoking 0.362 0.777 0.082 0.176 0.257
Ease 0.450 0.359 0.110 0.088 0.197
Critic 1.021 0.119 0.230 0.027 0.257
Surprise 0.265 0.126 0.072 0.034 0.106
Change 0.293 0.875 0.066 0.196 0.262
  • Non-independence is substantial for every construct. Reviewer and book together account for roughly 11% (Surprise) to 26% (Critic, Thought-Provoking, Change) of the latent variance. Treating the 49,823 reviews as independent, as the OLS t-tests did, therefore overstates precision.
  • The source of clustering differs by construct, which is substantively informative:
    • Reviewer-driven constructs: Critic (ICC reviewer = .23 vs. book = .03), Theme (.19 vs. .05) and Absence of Naive Realism (.15 vs. .05). Whether a review offers reasoned evaluation, interprets meaning, or acknowledges other viewpoints is largely a stable writing style of the reviewer, not a property of the book.
    • Book-driven constructs: Change (book = .20 vs. reviewer = .07) and Thought-Provoking (.18 vs. .08). Whether a review reports being made to think or having its author’s views changed depends more on which book was read.
    • Ease is split fairly evenly (.11 vs. .09); Surprise shows the least clustering of either kind.

7.3 Genre effects by construct

Odds ratios from the random-intercept models (*p < .05, **p < .01, ***p < .001):

or_wide <- res_all[res_all$term %in% genre_vars, ]
or_wide$cell <- sprintf("%.2f%s", or_wide$OR, or_wide$sig)
or_wide <- reshape(or_wide[, c("term", "outcome", "cell")], idvar = "term",
                   timevar = "outcome", direction = "wide")
names(or_wide) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(or_wide))
or_wide$term <- genre_labels[match(or_wide$term, genre_vars)]
knitr::kable(or_wide, row.names = FALSE)
term Absence_of_Naive_Realism Theme Thought_Provoking Ease Critic Surprise Change
Children 0.87* 0.85*** 0.74*** 1.47*** 0.63*** 0.72*** 0.72**
Comics & Graphic 0.65*** 0.74*** 0.67*** 1.38*** 0.74*** 0.79*** 0.61***
Fantasy & Paranormal 0.89*** 0.91*** 0.72*** 0.93** 1.08** 1.06* 0.56***
Fiction 1.26* 1.26** 1.19 0.93 1.06 0.99 1.09
History / Biography 1.14*** 1.17*** 1.09* 0.92** 1.09** 0.97 1.13
Mystery / Thriller / Crime 0.97 0.89*** 0.94 1.02 1.19*** 1.19*** 0.69***
Non-fiction 1.38*** 1.80*** 2.29*** 0.90 0.72*** 1.00 2.90***
Poetry 1.31* 1.32* 1.83*** 0.93 0.72** 0.81 1.02
Romance 0.72*** 0.68*** 0.51*** 1.24*** 0.95 1.02 0.51***
Young Adult 1.15*** 1.18*** 1.35*** 0.94* 1.10*** 1.16*** 1.46***

53 of the 70 genre coefficients are significant at p < .05. Read by genre, they form clear profiles:

  • Non-fiction: the strongest “reflective” profile. Non-fiction reviews have almost three times the odds of reporting a change in views (Change OR = 2.90***), and much higher odds of being Thought-Provoking (2.29***), discussing Theme (1.80***) and showing Absence of Naive Realism (1.38***). They are, however, less likely to contain craft-oriented Critic evaluation (0.72***). Ease and Surprise do not differ.
  • Poetry: similar but weaker. Higher odds of Thought-Provoking (1.83***), Theme (1.32*) and Absence of Naive Realism (1.31*), lower odds of Critic (0.72**). Poetry is the smallest category (about 500 reviews), so its intervals are wide.
  • Young Adult: consistently positive. Higher odds on six of seven constructs: Change (1.46***), Thought-Provoking (1.35***), Theme (1.18***), Surprise (1.16***), Absence of Naive Realism (1.15***) and Critic (1.10***); only Ease is slightly lower (0.94*).
  • History / Biography: modestly reflective. Higher Theme (1.17***), Absence of Naive Realism (1.14***), Critic (1.09**) and Thought-Provoking (1.09*); lower Ease (0.92**).
  • Romance: easy, but less reflective. The highest-ease adult genre (Ease 1.24***), but about half the odds of Thought-Provoking (0.51***) and Change (0.51***), and lower Theme (0.68***) and Absence of Naive Realism (0.72***). Critic and Surprise do not differ.
  • Children and Comics & Graphic: easy, but lower on everything else. These are the two genres with the highest Ease (1.47*** and 1.38***), and they are significantly lower on all six other constructs (ORs between 0.61 and 0.87).
  • Mystery / Thriller / Crime: surprise and critique. Higher Surprise (1.19***) and Critic (1.19***), consistent with plot-twist-driven reading, but lower Change (0.69***) and Theme (0.89***).
  • Fantasy & Paranormal: slightly less reflective. Lower Change (0.56***), Thought-Provoking (0.72***), Theme (0.91***), Absence of Naive Realism (0.89***) and Ease (0.93**); marginally higher Critic (1.08**) and Surprise (1.06*).
  • Fiction applies to about 98% of books, so its effect is weakly identified; it is significant only for Absence of Naive Realism (1.26*) and Theme (1.26**).

7.4 Patterns across constructs

genre_only <- res_all[res_all$term %in% genre_vars, ]
cross <- data.frame(
  genre        = genre_labels,
  n_sig_up     = sapply(genre_vars, function(g) sum(genre_only$term == g & genre_only$p_value < .05 & genre_only$OR > 1)),
  n_sig_down   = sapply(genre_vars, function(g) sum(genre_only$term == g & genre_only$p_value < .05 & genre_only$OR < 1)),
  n_ns         = sapply(genre_vars, function(g) sum(genre_only$term == g & genre_only$p_value >= .05)),
  row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(cross, col.names = c("Genre combination", "# constructs higher (p<.05)",
                                  "# constructs lower (p<.05)", "# not significant"))
Genre combination # constructs higher (p<.05) # constructs lower (p<.05) # not significant
Children 1 6 0
Comics & Graphic 1 6 0
Fantasy & Paranormal 2 5 0
Fiction 2 0 5
History / Biography 4 1 2
Mystery / Thriller / Crime 2 2 3
Non-fiction 4 1 2
Poetry 3 1 3
Romance 1 4 2
Young Adult 6 1 0
  1. An ease-reflection trade-off. The genres that make reading feel easiest (Children, Comics & Graphic, Romance) are the ones whose reviews are least likely to be thought-provoking, thematic or view-changing. Non-fiction and Poetry show the reverse pattern. At the genre level, Ease behaves almost as a mirror image of the reflective constructs.
  2. Change and Thought-Provoking are the most genre-sensitive constructs (widest OR range, 0.51 to 2.90), consistent with their book-level ICCs being the largest: these experiences depend on what is read.
  3. Critic follows a different logic. It is higher for plot-driven genres (Mystery 1.19, Young Adult 1.10, Fantasy 1.08) and lower for Non-fiction, Poetry and Children, and its clustering is almost entirely at the reviewer level. Critical evaluation appears to be more a property of the reviewer and of narrative genres than of intellectually demanding content.
  4. Surprise is the least genre-dependent construct (5 significant effects, the lowest ICCs), and is mainly elevated for Mystery / Thriller / Crime and Young Adult.

7.5 Comparison with the OLS models (genre_lm_ttests.qmd)

  • After accounting for reviewer and book, 53 of 70 genre effects remain significant, compared with 56 in OLS. All 53 GLMM-significant effects were also significant in OLS, and the direction of the effect agrees for 69 of 70 coefficients. The one disagreement (Poetry on Change) is null in both models.
  • Three effects lose significance in the nAGQ = 0 models: Fiction on Thought-Provoking (OLS p = .002, GLMM p = .064), Mystery / Thriller / Crime on Thought-Provoking (p < .001, GLMM p = .057) and Romance on Critic (p < .001, GLMM p = .099). With the more accurate Laplace fit (nAGQ = 1, Section 8) all three return to p < .05 (p = .028, .034, .034). They are therefore borderline effects whose significance depends on the estimation method and should be reported with caution rather than as clear differences.
  • The substantive conclusions are therefore robust; modelling non-independence mainly corrects the over-precision of the OLS estimates.

7.6 Interpretation notes

  • Genre is a book-level variable, so its effects are estimated mainly from differences between books; the book random intercept captures remaining book-to-book differences not explained by genre.
  • Each OR compares books with a genre combination to books without it, holding the other nine combinations constant. The intercept (a book with none of the ten combinations) does not occur in the data and should not be interpreted.
  • Odds ratios are conditional (reviewer- and book-specific) effects, so they are typically larger in magnitude than population-averaged effects from the OLS models in genre_lm_ttests.qmd.
  • Change (≈3% coded 1) and Absence of Naive Realism (≈14%) are rare outcomes; their CIs are wider, especially for small genres such as Poetry (n ≈ 500) and Non-fiction (n ≈ 1,700).
  • Outcomes are GPT-4o codes (v1 prompts), so effects describe how the AI coder labels reviews; any systematic coder error that correlates with genre would also appear here.

8. Robustness: nAGQ = 0 vs nAGQ = 1 (Laplace)

The main results use nAGQ = 0, which estimates the fixed effects inside the penalised iteratively re-weighted least-squares step (fast). nAGQ = 1 (Laplace approximation) optimises the fixed effects and variance components jointly on the approximate likelihood (slow, more accurate). The nAGQ = 1 models were fitted with the nAGQ = 0 estimates as starting values.

have_nagq1 <- all(file.exists(sprintf("nAGQ1/models/g%d_nagq1.rds", 1:7)))
have_nagq1
[1] TRUE
outcome_names <- c("Absence_of_Naive_Realism", "Theme", "Thought_Provoking", "Ease",
                   "Critic", "Surprise", "Change")
m1_list <- lapply(1:7, function(k) readRDS(sprintf("nAGQ1/models/g%d_nagq1.rds", k)))

res_all_1 <- do.call(rbind, Map(make_table, m1_list, outcome_names))
re_all_1  <- do.call(rbind, Map(make_re_table, m1_list, outcome_names))
write.csv(res_all_1, "nAGQ1/genre_glmer_coefficients_nagq1.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(re_all_1,  "nAGQ1/genre_glmer_random_effects_nagq1.csv", row.names = FALSE)

cmp <- merge(res_all[, c("outcome", "term", "log_odds", "std_error", "p_value", "sig")],
             res_all_1[, c("outcome", "term", "log_odds", "std_error", "p_value", "sig")],
             by = c("outcome", "term"), suffixes = c("_q0", "_q1"))

cmp$diff_log_odds <- cmp$log_odds_q1 - cmp$log_odds_q0

  • Coefficients whose significance differs: Thought_Provoking / fiction (p = 0.064 vs 0.028); Thought_Provoking / mystery_thriller_crime (p = 0.057 vs 0.034); Critic / romance (p = 0.099 vs 0.034); Surprise / poetry (p = 0.059 vs 0.047); Change / children (p = 0.007 vs 0.398); Change / comics_graphic (p = 0.000 vs 0.196); Change / fantasy_paranormal (p = 0.000 vs 0.114); Change / mystery_thriller_crime (p = 0.000 vs 0.980); Change / non_fiction (p = 0.000 vs 0.078); Change / romance (p = 0.000 vs 0.420); Change / young_adult (p = 0.000 vs 0.362)

8.2 Conclusions of the robustness check

  • For six of the seven constructs the two methods agree almost perfectly. The genre coefficients correlate at r > .999 within every one of these models, the largest difference is 0.18 on the log-odds scale, every sign is the same, and the random-effect SDs are similar (the Laplace fit gives slightly larger variances, most visibly for books in Absence of Naive Realism: SD 0.44 vs. 0.58).
  • Four borderline coefficients cross p = .05, all from just above to just below: Fiction and Mystery / Thriller / Crime on Thought-Provoking (p = .064 → .028; .057 → .034), Romance on Critic (.099 → .034) and Poetry on Surprise (.059 → .047). None of the clearly significant effects changes. These four should be described as weak or borderline.
  • The nAGQ = 1 fit of Change is degenerate and should not be used. Both random-intercept SDs explode to about 27 on the logit scale (vs. 0.94 and 0.54 with nAGQ = 0), the intercept moves from −3.0 to −30.9, and the genre standard errors inflate 20- to 50-fold, so no genre effect is significant and some odds ratios become absurd (e.g. Non-fiction OR = 355). This is a known failure of the Laplace approximation for rare binary outcomes with many singleton clusters: only 3% of reviews are coded Change = 1, and 32% of reviewers and 44% of books contribute a single review, so the approximate likelihood keeps “improving” as each positive review is absorbed into its own random effect. The higher log-likelihood of this fit (−5045 vs. −6285) is an artefact of the approximation, not a better model. The optimiser reports convergence only because it stopped, not because it found a valid estimate.
  • Recommendation: report the nAGQ = 0 models as the main results (Sections 4–7), mention that the Laplace fits confirm them for six constructs, and treat the Change model’s variance components with caution. If a stricter check for Change is needed, a model with a weakly informative prior on the random-effect variances (e.g. blme::bglmer), or a reviewer-only or book-only random intercept, would avoid the degenerate solution.
